interest: This file provides valuable insight into the clandestine mechanisms of Japanese territorial and military penetration in North China following the 1933 Tanggu Truce. It highlights how major Japanese commercial zaibatsu firms, specifically Okura and Company, operated alongside the Japanese military garrison to acquire large tracts of land under the guise of agricultural enterprises (such as vineyards and vegetable gardens) while suspected of preparing military infrastructure like airfields. The documents also illustrate the vigilance and investigative role of the local Chinese vernacular press (such as I Shih Pao and Ta Kung Pao), the legal pushback by traditional Chinese charitable gentry corporations (Kwang Jen T'ang), and the active intelligence monitoring maintained by U.S. consular and diplomatic officials in Tientsin and Peiping.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.24593, covering October 1933 to April 1936) documents U.S. diplomatic monitoring of reported Japanese plans to construct a military airdrome at Nankai near Tientsin, China. In October 1933, local Chinese vernacular newspapers reported that the Japanese military garrison at Haikuangssu had acquired over 1,000 mou of land at Liulit'ai through Japanese firm Okura and Company and local Chinese figures to construct an aviation base. Subsequent investigations reported by American Consul General Frank P. Lockhart revealed that the land belonged to the Chinese charitable foundation Kwang Jen T'ang, which contested the unauthorized lease, prompting local Chinese municipal authorities to block the construction. While Japanese officials and Okura and Company insisted the project was merely an agricultural enterprise and sought diplomatic redress for interrupted work, the file concludes with a 1936 cross-reference sheet indicating continued U.S. surveillance over expanding Japanese barracks and airfield construction in Tientsin.

subfiles.about: Covering despatch transmitting a consular report on reported Japanese plans to construct an airdrome at Nankai near Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: American Consul General F. P. Lockhart in Tientsin transmits in quintuplicate to the Secretary of State his Despatch No. 482 of October 9, 1933, addressed to the American Legation at Peiping. The despatch concerns press reports alleging Japanese plans to build an aerodrome at Nankai. Copies were directed to the Office of Naval Intelligence (O.N.I.) and the Military Intelligence Division (M.I.D.).
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 417 from Lockhart (Tientsin) transmitting report on reported Japanese plans for airdrome at Nankai

subfiles.about: Consular report detailing press reports, land transactions, and investigations concerning an alleged Japanese military airdrome at Liulit'ai, Nankai.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Lockhart reports to Minister Nelson T. Johnson on Chinese press coverage alleging that the Japanese military acquired 1,050 mou of land at Liulit'ai near Haikuangssu barracks to construct an aviation field for 1,000 aircraft. The tract was leased from Yang Chih-hsiang and Hsu Shou-lin without the sanction of the legal owners, the Chinese charitable institution Kwang Jen T'ang. Although five hundred laborers began clearing work under Japanese firm Okura and Company, Chinese municipal authorities halted the project, and the Japanese military subsequently gave assurances that no aerodrome was planned.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 482 from Lockhart (Tientsin) to Johnson (Peiping) on reported Japanese airdrome at Nankai

subfiles.about: Internal State Department routing slip noting that no action was required regarding Lockhart's report on the Nankai airdrome.
subfiles.summary: An internal routing memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs in the Department of State circulating Despatch No. 417. The document directs officers JEJ, RCD, and SJF to note the contents of the report and concludes that no official action was required.
subfiles.title: State Department Far Eastern Affairs Division routing slip regarding Tientsin airdrome report

subfiles.about: Covering despatch transmitting a follow-up report on developments surrounding the disputed Nankai land tract.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Lockhart sends Despatch No. 430 to the Secretary of State, referencing his earlier Despatch No. 417 of October 1933. He transmits copies of follow-up Despatch No. 491 sent to the Legation at Peiping on October 28, 1933, reporting additional information on the alleged airdrome site.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 430 from Lockhart (Tientsin) transmitting further report on Nankai airdrome

subfiles.about: Consular despatch reporting on the commercial agricultural partnership between Yang Chih-hsiang and Okura and Company and subsequent diplomatic representations.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart updates Minister Johnson using details from the I Shih Pao, reporting that Yang Chih-hsiang rented 1,055 mou from Kwang Jen T'ang and formed an agricultural development firm with Okura and Company capitalized at $200,000. After work was stopped by Chinese authorities on October 1, Okura and Company asked the Japanese Consulate General to file a financial damages claim. The Japanese Consul General and Okura's manager planned to meet the provincial Governor to request permission to proceed under renewed assurances that no aerodrome would be built.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 491 from Lockhart (Tientsin) to Johnson (Peiping) on Okura and Company land dispute at Nankai

subfiles.about: Document file note cross-referencing a 1936 despatch from Johnson concerning Japanese barracks and an aviation field at Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State Document File Note referencing decimal file 793.94/7904 for Despatch No. 396 dated April 22, 1936, from American Minister Nelson T. Johnson in China. The referenced document relates to the construction of Japanese barracks and an aviation field in Tientsin.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for despatch No. 396 regarding Japanese barracks and aviation field at Tientsin
